name: ACPL-C79A-500E
title: ACPL-C79x family (C79B, C79A, C790): optically isolated precision amplifier, gain 8.2, 200 kHz, SSO-8
summary: An isolation amplifier for current and voltage sensing across a high-voltage barrier. A sigma-delta modulator on the input side sends the signal optically to the output side, which delivers a differential voltage 8.2 times the differential input, centred on about 1.23 V. The input side runs from 4.5 V to 5.5 V and the output side from 3 V to 5.5 V; nominal input is ±200 mV with ±300 mV full scale. The three grades are specified for gain tolerance: ±0.5 % for ACPL-C79B, ±1 % for ACPL-C79A and ±3 % for ACPL-C790. The package is a stretched SO-8 with 8 mm creepage and clearance, rated 5000 Vrms for one minute.

circuits.title: Motor phase current sensing
circuits.description: One phase leg of a motor inverter carries its motor current through a shunt, RSENSE. A 78L05 (U1) takes the floating supply that also feeds the high-side gate driver down to 5 V for VDD1. The shunt voltage reaches VIN+ through a 10 Ω / 47 nF low-pass (R5, C3); VIN- and GND1 both return to the negative end of the shunt, which is the phase node. On the isolated side a TL032A (U3) on ±15 V, with 2.00 kΩ input and 10.0 kΩ feedback resistors, turns the differential output into one voltage referred to GND2; C5 and C6 across the 10.0 kΩ resistors set a single low-pass pole. C2 and C4 bypass the two supplies at the pins.
notes: Q1, Q2, the gate drive circuit and the motor stand for one leg of the motor drive; the lines marked *** continue to the rest of the drive.
GND1 has no other connection to the gate-drive circuit than through the shunt's negative end; the positive floating supply is the only other shared line.

circuits.title: Differential (balanced) input connection
circuits.description: Both inputs are driven through equal series resistors, Ra on VIN+ and Rb on VIN-, with a capacitor C between the two pins. The switching currents of the two inputs then balance in the filter resistors, and noise picked up on one input is coupled to the other by C so that it appears as common mode, which the amplifier rejects. Typical values are 10 Ω for Ra and Rb and 22 nF for C.
notes: Only the input side, pins 1 to 4, belongs to this connection.

operation.text: The input side converts the differential input to a bit stream with a sigma-delta modulator built from chopper-stabilized, fully differential stages; the bit stream crosses the barrier as light and the output side rebuilds a differential analog voltage. A shield sits between the two halves. Each side has its own supply and ground.
ACPL-C79B (±0.5 % gain) is the precision grade; ACPL-C79A (±1 %) and ACPL-C790 (±3 %) are the general-purpose grades.
Gain is the slope of the straight line fitted to VOUT+ - VOUT- against VIN+ - VIN- across the nominal input range, after removing offset.
Nonlinearity is half the peak-to-peak departure of the output from that fitted line, as a percentage of full-scale differential output.
CMRRIN, in dB, compares the gain for a differential signal with the gain for a signal applied to both inputs tied together, measured against GND1.

CMTI is measured by stepping GND1 (pin 4) against GND2 (pin 5) with an exponential edge of about 50 ns rise time and raising the amplitude until the differential output departs from its average by more than 200 mV for longer than 1 µs. Common-mode slopes beyond 10 kV/µs do not stop the device working, within its breakdown voltage limits.
PSR is the differential ripple at the output, referred to the input, divided by the ripple on the supply, in dB.

Specified accuracy holds over ±200 mV. The output follows the input up to ±300 mV full scale; past it each output clamps, VOUT+ near 2.5 V and VOUT- near 0 V (or the reverse). The functional input range is ±2 V.
The inputs are a fully differential switched-capacitor circuit; the input bias current figures are time averages.

Each side needs a 0.1 µF capacitor right at its pins, VDD1 to GND1 and VDD2 to GND2, because of the fast digital signals inside. VDD1 is usually derived from the gate-drive supply of the power transistor, for example through a 78L05; a series resistor or inductor ahead of the regulator, with its input capacitor, filters high-frequency ripple. Alternatives are an extra transformer winding, a mains transformer or a small high-frequency isolated DC-DC converter.

A 47 nF capacitor across the input pins is recommended because the input is switched-capacitor. With the series resistor it forms an anti-aliasing low-pass that keeps high-frequency noise from folding into the signal band, and it limits ESD transients entering through the shunt.

In the single-ended connection VIN+ goes to the positive end of the shunt and VIN- is tied to GND1, and the supply return wire acts as the sense lead to the negative end. One pair of wires then serves, and load-current noise on the shunt appears as common mode. If the gate drive and the amplifier share a supply, the GND1-to-shunt link must be the only return path for the gate-drive supply current, to avoid ground loops; the positive supply line is the only other connection between the two circuits.

The shunt should have low resistance for low dissipation, low inductance so di/dt spikes stay small, and a tolerance in keeping with overall accuracy. A larger value uses more of the input range and improves accuracy; a smaller value cuts dissipation but makes the fixed offset and noise a larger share of the signal.

When the shunt heats noticeably its temperature coefficient adds signal-dependent nonlinearity, worse with higher thermal resistance to ambient; lower thermal resistance (placement, wider copper, a heat sink) or a lower-tempco part reduces it. In two-terminal shunts of low value the leads become a significant part of the resistance, making it depend on lead length, bending, insertion depth and solder wicking, and raising the overall tempco because copper leads have a higher tempco than the element. A four-terminal (Kelvin) shunt removes both effects.

Bring the Kelvin traces together under the shunt body and run them close to each other to the amplifier input to keep the loop area small against stray magnetic fields; off board, a tightly twisted pair does the same. Multiple layers of 2 oz or 4 oz copper, with many plated vias around each non-Kelvin terminal, give current capacity above 20 A; large traces, and many vias at the points of entry and exit of the load current, also help carry heat away.

Larger voltages are sensed through a resistive divider at the input. The divider impedance should be under 1 kΩ so the 22 kΩ input resistance and 0.1 µA bias current do not spoil accuracy. The input capacitor is still needed; the 10 Ω series resistor is not, since the divider provides the damping. The divider resistance and input capacitor form a low-pass that may limit bandwidth.

The op-amp after the isolation amplifier should have offset and offset drift small compared with the amplifier's own; bipolar-input op-amps generally beat JFET or MOSFET inputs on offset. It also needs enough bandwidth and slew rate not to slow the circuit. C5 and C6 set a single-pole low-pass independently of the gain and reduce output noise. Gain resistors of 1 % tolerance or better keep CMRR and gain tolerance adequate; a resistor network gives tighter ratios, fewer parts and less board area.

Stray capacitance from the input circuit to the output circuit degrades CMTI. Keep the input and output sides as far apart as possible and do not let any ground or power plane run under the package or extend much beyond its body. Keep bypass capacitors close to the supply pins and output traces away from input traces. In the example layout C2 sits at pins 1 and 4, C4 at pins 8 and 5, R5 and C3 at the input pins, with the shunt traces entering on the left and VOUT+ and VOUT- leaving on the right.
Reflow follows JEDEC J-STD-020 (latest revision) for lead-free soldering; use non-halide flux.
The device is ESD sensitive and needs normal static precautions. It is not for military or aerospace use.
